thinkBeforeYouCode.question: Why does standard HashMap fail as an LRU cache, and how does LinkedHashMap solve it with O(1) complexity?
thinkBeforeYouCode.mentorInsight: HashMap has no concept of element ordering; finding the least-recently used key would require scanning every entry in O(N) time. LinkedHashMap maintains a hidden doubly-linked list through all hash buckets. With accessOrder=true, every get() or put() unlinks the accessed node and splices it to the tail in O(1) time.

thinkBeforeYouCode.question: What happens if get() is called on an expired entry? Should it return null or Optional.empty()?
thinkBeforeYouCode.mentorInsight: Returning Optional.empty() forces calling code to handle cache misses explicitly without risking NullPointerException, adhering to modern clean API design.

thinkBeforeYouCode.question: Why is Collections.synchronizedMap() or explicit synchronization needed around an access-order LinkedHashMap even for read-only get() calls?
thinkBeforeYouCode.mentorInsight: In access-order mode, get() is structurally a WRITE operation! It modifies the internal doubly-linked list pointers to reorder nodes. Multiple concurrent get() calls without synchronization will corrupt pointers and trigger infinite loops.

activities.title: Practical Context: Desk Workspace vs Warehouse Archival
activities.description: Why fixed-capacity LRU caching is critical for high-throughput computing.
activities.content:
Imagine an analyst working at a physical desk that holds exactly 5 reference folders. When they need a folder, they grab it from the warehouse archive (database) and place it on top of their desk (cache). As new folders arrive, the desk fills up.

When the desk is full and a 6th folder is needed, the analyst doesn't throw away a random file; they return the folder sitting at the very bottom that hasn't been touched in the longest time (Least Recently Used). If an old folder has an expiration stamp that has lapsed (TTL), it is shredded immediately.

An In-Memory LRU Cache replicates this physical workspace: keeping hot records on the fast CPU/heap desk while deterministically bounding memory usage and evicting cold data in O(1) time.

activities.title: Architecture of an LRU Cache with LinkedHashMap
activities.description: Technical deep dive into access-order doubly-linked lists and removeEldestEntry mechanics.
activities.content:
### Formal Computer Science Definition
A Least-Recently-Used (LRU) Cache is a bounded associative key-value store that evicts the item that has not been accessed for the longest duration whenever insertion exceeds maximum capacity. It guarantees $O(1)$ amortized lookup, insertion, and eviction.

### Architectural Diagram

```
                                 LruCache<K, V>
                                       |
       +-------------------------------+-------------------------------+
       |                                                               |
Hash Table (HashMap)                                      Doubly-Linked List
- Bucket-indexed fast lookup O(1)                         - Maintains access ordering
- Stores Key -> Node references                           - Head = Least Recently Used (LRU)
                                                          - Tail = Most Recently Used (MRU)
                                                                       |
       +---------------------------------------------------------------+ 
       |  When get(K) is called: Node unlinked and spliced to Tail (MRU)
       |  When put(K, V) exceeds capacity: Head node (LRU) evicted in O(1)
```

### Key Contracts & Implementation Rules
1. **`super(capacity, 0.75f, true)`**: Passing `true` for `accessOrder` instructs `LinkedHashMap` to re-splice nodes to the tail on every `get()` and `put()`.
2. **`removeEldestEntry(entry)`**: Invoked by `put()` automatically. Returning `size() > maxCapacity` triggers automatic head node removal.
3. **Concurrency Warning**: Access-order `get()` mutates internal pointers! It must be synchronized to prevent race conditions.

questions.question: Why must get() calls be synchronized when using LinkedHashMap in access-order mode?
options: Because get() hashes keys using multi-threaded crypto algorithms
Because get() modifies the pointers of the underlying doubly-linked list to move the accessed node to the tail
Because LinkedHashMap throws UnsupportedOperationException if unsynchronized
Because Java 21 enforces synchronization on all Map subclasses
questions.explanation: In access-order mode (accessOrder=true), get() is structurally a write operation that unlinks the accessed node and splices it to the MRU tail. Concurrent unsynchronized get() calls will corrupt pointers, creating infinite loops.

questions.question: What is the amortized time complexity for get(), put(), and eviction in an LRU cache backed by LinkedHashMap?
options: O(N) for get, O(1) for put
O(1) for get, put, and eviction
O(1) for get, O(N) for eviction
questions.explanation: LinkedHashMap combines hash table bucket indexing (O(1) lookup) with doubly-linked list node splicing (O(1) relocation and head eviction), achieving O(1) amortized complexity for all core operations.

questions.question: What does removeEldestEntry() receive as an argument?
options: The Map.Entry that was least-recently accessed (at the head of the linked list)
The Map.Entry that was just inserted
The integer size of the cache
questions.explanation: removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) receives the eldest entry (the node at the head of the doubly-linked list), allowing custom eviction criteria based on key, value, or size.

questions.question: Compare LRU (Least Recently Used) with LFU (Least Frequently Used) and FIFO cache eviction strategies.
questions.answer:
1. FIFO (First-In, First-Out): Evicts the oldest inserted entry regardless of access patterns. Trivial to implement (queue) but performs poorly when old items remain hot.
2. LRU (Least Recently Used): Evicts the item whose last access timestamp is oldest. Highly effective for temporal locality workloads where recently used items are likely to be accessed again soon. Implemented via LinkedHashMap in O(1).
3. LFU (Least Frequently Used): Evicts the item with the lowest access count. Excellent for frequency stability, but susceptible to cache pollution from burst items that become cold, and requires more complex O(1) double-linked bucket structures.

questions.question: How would you implement a thread-safe LRU cache without synchronizing on every get() call?
questions.answer:
To eliminate read contention in high-throughput systems:
1. Use ConcurrentHashMap for lock-free O(1) key-value storage.
2. Maintain access ordering using a concurrent ring buffer or striped thread-local queues that record access events asynchronously.
3. A single maintenance thread (or worker thread during write) drains the access queues and updates the recency list, eliminating read locks entirely (similar to caffeine/Guava cache design).
